stops.name: Quierzy, the keys of the tomb of Saint Peter
stops.campa: An embassy such as Frankland has never seen comes over the Alps: Pope Gregory III, pressed by the Lombards, sends Charles the keys of the tomb of Saint Peter and a link of the Apostle's chains, begging him to defend Rome: offering to turn Peter from the emperor in Constantinople to the mayor of the Franks. Charles receives the keys with honor, sends Abbot Grimo and Sigebert of Saint-Denis to Rome with gifts, and does not march: Liutprand is his sworn friend, his son's arms-father. The rescue is refused; the door is left open. Through it his sons and grandson will walk to a crown.
stops.quote: He sent to the prince the keys of the venerable tomb and the chains of Saint Peter, with great and countless gifts, such as had never before been seen or heard of.

stops.name: Quierzy, the realm divided like a king's
stops.campa: Feeling his strength ebb, Charles does what only kings had done. With the counsel of his magnates he divides the realm between his sons: Austrasia, Alemannia and Thuringia to Carloman; Neustria, Burgundy and Provence to Pepin, with lordship over Aquitaine and Bavaria at the edges. To Grifo, Swanachild's son, a middle portion that will not hold. There is no king to confirm the act and none is needed; the division itself is the crown he never wore, exercised as plainly as a man dividing his own field.

stops.name: Quierzy on the Oise, the death of the Hammer
stops.campa: At his palace of Quierzy on the Oise, in fever, Charles dies on 22 October 741, aged about fifty-three: mayor of the palace, prince of the Franks, ruler of a kingdom with no king, unbeaten from Amblève to the Berre save once by Radbod's Frisians when he had nothing but his name. The chronicle gives him death in peace: the one engagement he does not choose the ground for. The realm he leaves is not the realm he was jailed in: it is a single forged thing, and it bears his hammer-mark.

stops.name: Saint-Denis: a king in all but name, among the kings
stops.campa: They carry him down the Oise and lay him in the abbey of Saint-Denis, among the Merovingian kings, a bastard mayor buried in the royal necropolis, the stone itself pronouncing what the diadem never did. From his body the line runs forward: Pepin crowned within a decade, Charlemagne named for him, the Chanson's Christendom armed in his image. And south of Tours, behind a village altar, a sword with five crosses settles into its seven hundred years of rust, waiting for the girl. The Hammer rests; the iron remembers.
